title: Polynomial Bounds for the Graph Minor Structure Theorem
authors: Maximilian Gorsky (Discrete Mathematics Group, Institute for Basic Science (IBS), South Korea), Michal T. Seweryn (Computer Science Institute, Charles University, Czech Republic), Sebastian Wiederrecht (School of Computing, KAIST, South Korea)
abstract: The Graph Minor Structure Theorem, originally proven by Robertson and Seymour [JCTB, 2003], asserts that there exist functions f_1, f_2 N → N such that for every non-planar graph H with t := |V(H)|, every H-minor-free graph can be obtained via the clique-sum operation from graphs which embed into surfaces where H does not embed after deleting at most f_1(t) many vertices with up to at most t^2 - 1 many "vortices" which are of "depth" at most f_2(t). In the proof presented by Robertson and Seymour the functions f_1 and f_2 are non-constructive. Kawarabayashi, Thomas, and Wollan [arXiv, 2020] found a new proof showing that f_1(t), f_2(t) ∊ 2^{poly(t)}. While believing that this bound was the best their methods could achieve, Kawarabayashi, Thomas, and Wollan conjectured that f_1 and f_2 can be improved to be polynomials. In this paper we confirm their conjecture and prove that f_1(t), f_2(t) ∊ O(t^{2300}). Our proofs are fully constructive and yield a polynomial-time algorithm that either finds H as a minor in a graph G or produces a clique-sum decomposition for G as above.

Abstract—The Graph Minor Structure Theorem, originally
proven by Robertson and Seymour [JCTB, 2003], asserts that
there exist functions f1 , f2 : N → N such that for every nonplanar graph H with t := |V (H)|, every H-minor-free graph
can be obtained via the clique-sum operation from graphs which
embed into surfaces where H does not embed after deleting
at most f1 (t) many vertices with up to at most t2 − 1 many
“vortices” which are of “depth” at most f2 (t). In the proof
presented by Robertson and Seymour the functions f1 and f2 are
non-constructive. Kawarabayashi, Thomas, and Wollan [arXiv,
2020] found a new proof showing that f1 (t), f2 (t) ∈ 2poly(t) .
While believing that this bound was the best their methods could
achieve, Kawarabayashi, Thomas, and Wollan conjectured that
f1 and f2 can be improved to be polynomials.
In this paper we confirm their conjecture and prove that
f1 (t), f2 (t) ∈ O(t2300 ). Our proofs are fully constructive and
yield a polynomial-time algorithm that either finds H as a minor
in a graph G or produces a clique-sum decomposition for G as
above.
Index Terms—structural graph theory, minor, algorithms, fixed
parameter tractability, graph minor structure theorem

I. I NTRODUCTION
A graph H is a minor of a graph G if it can be obtained
from a subgraph of G by contracting edges. There are many
instances of graph classes where graphs excluding particular
minors share a specific, restricted structure. For example, K3 minor-free graphs are forests, and by Wagner’s Theorem [1],
graphs excluding K5 and K3,3 as minors are planar. These
two examples can be seen as special cases of two theorems
that sit at the heart of the monumental Graph Minors Series by
Robertson and Seymour (R&S), namely the Grid Theorem [2]
and the Graph Minor Structure Theorem (GMST ) [3] (see [4]
for a summary of both results written by R&S). The former
describes the structure of graphs excluding planar graphs as
minors (such as K3 ), and the latter explains the structure of
graphs excluding non-planar graphs as minors.
These two theorems are widely regarded to be among
the deepest results in graph theory and their importance for
structural graph theory, graph algorithms, and parameterized
complexity can hardly be overstated [5]–[12]. There has been
considerable effort in the community to simplify the proofs

So far this statement has remained true as only a single

Our result. We show that the functions involved in the
GMST are polynomials in the size of the excluded minor,
confirming the conjecture of KTW. Our proofs are fully
constructive and lead to a polynomial-time algorithm.
In addition, we also confirm two conjectures of Wollan [12]:
The first conjecture is a further strengthening of the result of
KTW [18], confirming polynomial bounds and tight bounds on
the Euler-genus of the surfaces involved. The second asks for
polynomial bounds on a theorem of R&S on minors of graphs
with highly representative embeddings (Theorem 4.3 in [22])
for which previously no constructive bounds were known.
Both the Grid Theorem and the GMST act as rough descriptions of graphs excluding a fixed graph H as a minor
and a simple way to reformulate those theorems is through
the use of so-called “clique-sums”. A graph G is a clique-sum
of two graphs G1 and G2 if there exist cliques2 Xi ⊆ V (Gi ),
i ∈ {1, 2}, where |X1 | = |X2 | and G can be obtained from
G1 and G2 by identifying the vertices of X1 and X2 and then
possibly deleting some of the edges between the vertices of
X1 = X2 .
Roughly speaking, the Grid Theorem says that there exists
a function grid such that for every planar graph H, any graph
excluding H as a minor can be obtained via clique-sums from

Our main result and thus the GMST reads as follows (see
the full version [25] for a precise statement).
Theorem 1.1: There exists a function clique : N → N, with
clique(t) ∈ O(t2300 ), such that for every non-planar graph
H, every H-minor-free graph G can be obtained by means of
clique-sums from graphs that are clique(|H|)-near embeddable
into surfaces where H does not embed.
In order to prove Theorem 1.1 we begin with a simplified
proof for the so-called Flat Wall Theorem, also known as the
“Weak Structure Theorem”, which first appeared in [26] as
Theorem 9.8. In addition to this, we obtain a new proof for
the so-called Local Structure Theorem (LST), also known as
the “structure with respect to a tangle”, which appeared in its
original form as Theorem 3.1 in [3]. Our version of the LST
enjoys the same qualities, including the polynomial bounds,
as our main theorem. Indeed one may regard the new bounds
for the LST as our true main result.
Both theorems, the Flat Wall and the LST, are much
more technical in nature than the statement of Theorem 1.1.
Nonetheless they are key tools for the design of many algorithms on H-minor-free graphs (see for example [11], [26],
[27]) as they give rise to the so-called Irrelevant Vertex
Technique [28]. Beyond algorithmic applications, even the
proof of well-quasi-ordering for graph minors builds on a
different kind of “globalisation” of the LST [29] rather than
the GMST itself. R&S point this out themselves in [3] where
they refer to the GMST as a “red herring” and explain that all
of their own future applications are based on the LST.
Similar to the situation regarding the Grid Theorem, the
Flat Wall Theorem has enjoyed quite a lot of improvements
over the time [20], [30]–[32]. The LST on the other hand is
so closely related to the full GMST that the sole significant
progress is again the one of KTW [18]. Our new proof of the
LST establishes polynomial bounds on all involved functions.
This has immediate consequences on the parametric dependencies in the running times of most (if not all) algorithmic
applications of this theorem.

a) A short history of explicit bounds for R&S’ theory
of graph minors.: The original proof for the Grid Theorem
can be found in [2], while the GMST was established in
[3], but requires the theory and many results proven in the
preceding 15 papers of the series. Both proofs only establish
existence for the functions grid and clique. Figure 1 presents
a timeline of the milestones regarding explicit bounds for the
Grid Theorem and the GMST. The first explicit bound for
grid was proven by Robertson, Seymour, and Thomas [13],
establishing grid(t) ∈ 2poly(t) . Some follow-up work was
concerned with improving the polynomial in the exponent
[14], [16]. In their breakthrough result, Chekuri and Chuzhoy
[15] achieved the next leap by proving grid(t) ∈ poly(t).
This has since been improved by Chuzhoy and Tan [17] to
O(t9 polylog t).
The original statement of the GMST stems from R&S’
16th entry in the Graph Minors Series [29] and its proof
contains a single non-constructive argument towards the existence of clique. This argument was made constructive by
Geelen, Huynh, and Richter [33] without making the bound
for clique explicit. In their milestone papers, KTW [18], [20]
provide7 a proof of the GMST giving a first explicit bound
with clique(t) ∈ 2poly(t) . With their two papers, KTW also
achieved the feat of greatly simplifying the proof of the GMST.
However, the bound on the Euler-genus of the surfaces into
which their graphs may near embed is slightly worse than the
optimal bound on the Euler-genus of the surfaces “where H
does not embed”.
In [18] the authors conjecture that the bounds for the GMST
should be polynomials. Moreover, Wollan conjectured [12]
that in addition to polynomial bounds for the GMST, one can
simultaneously achieve the optimal bound on the Euler-genus.
This would then further imply a third conjecture, which asserts
that there exists a polynomial p such that for every graph H,
any graph G that can be embedded with representativity8 at
least p(|H|) into some surface Σ where H also embeds must
contain H as a minor [12]. In this paper, we resolve all three
conjectures.

II. S UFFICIENCY AND NECESSITY
Both the Grid Theorem and the GMST act as approximate
characterisations for H-minor-free graphs. However, so far
we have only emphasised the necessity for the arising cliquesum structure of H-minor-free graphs. A key aspect of both
theorems is that these rough descriptions are also sufficient
to capture the structure of H-minor-free graphs. To make this
precise, the Grid Theorem says that any graph with treewidth
at least grid(t) must contain the (t × t)-grid13 as a minor.
Now firstly, the (t × t)-grid is a planar graph for all t and
for every planar graph H there is tH ∈ O(|H|) [13] such
that H is a minor of the (tH × tH )-grid. Secondly, and this
is the sufficiency part, it is well known [2] that no graph that
contains the (t × t)-grid as a minor has treewidth less than t.
A similar statement holds for the GMST. However, instead
of the (t × t)-grid as the universal graph we now have to
consider the (non-)existence of a Kt -minor. Joret and Wood
[59] proved that there exists a constant c such that no graph
with a Kt -minor can be obtained via clique-sums from graphs
that are k-near embeddable
√ into surfaces of Euler-genus g for
any k with t > c(k + 1) g + k.

III. T HE L OCAL S TRUCTURE T HEOREM
Considering the discussion in Section II and the Grid
Theorem itself, it becomes clear that the only graphs where
the notion of near embeddability becomes relevant are those
of large treewidth, which is not visible in the statement of
Theorem 1.1. As discussed above, the centrepiece to achieving
the GMST is the LST [3], [26], [28], [34]. Indeed, we believe
that the LST is the heart of the entire graph minors theory
of R&S and its role is pivotal to most applications including
the majority of those mentioned above. Moreover, the LST
explicitly captures the interesting parts of the GMST as those
that exhibit large treewidth.
The LST describes the structure of graphs excluding a
minor “locally”. Informally, the theorem decomposes an Hminor-free “highly linked part” of a graph. In the original
formulation of the LST, a “highly-linked part” is formalised
by the concept of a “tangle”.16 Tangles found their use not
only in graphs, but also matroids, and more generally, artificial
intelligence and empirical sciences (see the recent book by
Diestel [63]). The statement of the LST due to KTW is
expressed in terms of walls instead of tangles. The benefit
of using walls is that they are more concrete, and in particular
they straightforwardly allow for efficient representation in

Hence, our local theorem describe the structure of a graph

As described in Section IV, two out of three sources

every step, and their way to deal with leaps by inductively
constructing leap patterns. Both of these can be fully avoided
by our approach through transaction meshes. However, as in
the original strategy of R&S and the proof of KTW, our own
approach hinges on the use of crooked transactions.
A fundamental step in each iteration is the one of orthogonalisation. Let us first describe what we mean by that and
then explain why this step is crucial.
As described above, both proofs, the one of KTW and
ours, rely fundamentally on iteratively finding large crooked
transactions. Once such a transaction is found, it has to go
through several “clean-up” steps to ensure that part of it can
be used to augment the current embedding. This is required,
among other things, for an application of a variant of the
Flat Wall Theorem. However, the keen observer will notice
that a transaction on its own neither is a mesh, nor does it
offer enough “horizontal” infrastructure to construct something
resembling a mesh. This is where the need for maintaining a

large nest comes from. Recall the diagram on the right of
Figure 7. Here we depict a grid-like infrastructure created

the nest is already embedded in a “flat” fashion. However, an
arbitrary crooked transaction in a society does not have to be
orthogonal to a given nest. See Figure 10 for a depiction of
two societies, one with an arbitrary crooked transaction, and
one with an orthogonal crooked transaction.

this question. In the simplest setting, we are interested in
algorithms, which given a graph of treewidth at least f (k)
find a model of the k-grid. However, as we have explain in
the full version [25], it is important to be able to not only

related to a given tangle or highly linked set. Kawarabayashi
et al. [18] derived an algorithm that finds a model related
to a given tangle of order roughly f (k 2 ), assuming that they

graph of treewidth f (k). It took us a considerable effort in the
full version [25] to derive an algorithm finding a wall related

to a given tangle of order Ω(k 98 polylog k), but for that we
had to dive into the details of the algorithm by [15]. For that
reason, we appeal to the brave researchers working on the Grid
Theorem to develop more “localised” algorithms which find a
grid-minor related to a given tangle, or a similar object, such
as a highly linked set.
Two advantages of highly linked sets over tangles is that
they have an efficient representation in computer memory, and
we can efficiently verify if a set is highly linked. Recall that
every (k, α)-linked set X determines a tangle of order Ω(k),
and any tangle of order k determines a well-linked set of order
Ω(k), which is (Ω(k), 23 )-linked. In this sense, tangles and
highly linked sets are “approximately equivalent”.

b) Finding a simpler proof.: One notable feature of the
KTW-proof of the GMST is that they endeavoured to keep
their proof elementary. In this context, elementary means that
all theorems not proven in their paper(s) can be found in
standard graph theory textbooks. Thus their paper should in
theory be accessible to graduate students or even particularly
determined undergraduate students. Note that in this context
[20] and [18] are considered to be a single continuous text
containing the proof of the GMST.
We did not attempt to put this restriction upon ourselves

and we are under no delusions that our proofs will be seen
as simple or elementary. Within our proof there are however
several ideas that we believe simplify the approach of KTW
if applied well and, while their proof was certainly a massive
leap forward, we do not believe that their approach can
be considered to be easy to understand either. Reiterating
Lovász’s statement from [8], we therefore still believe it would
be quite important to have a simpler proof of the GMST with
explicit bounds. In particular, a proof that is accessible to
graduate students – maybe even to undergraduate students –
and could be taught within one university semester would be
a very valuable addition to the literature. We believe that it
should be possible to find such a proof whilst still delivering
modest bounds for all the involved functions, meaning at worst
exponential but possibly even polynomial. As in the work of
KTW, this proof may even start from the assumption that the
Grid Theorem is true.
Here we want to also explicitly express a demand for a
simpler proof of the well-quasi ordering theorem for graph
minors [77]. This theorem is an important entry point for
a set of conjectures that expand on the well-quasi ordering
properties of graphs with respect to minors and other relations
(see [78], [79]). A more accessible proof would help to
facilitate more research in this important area of (meta) graph
theory.
c) Tight bounds.: The definition of Σ-decomposition
involves four parameters which should be bounded in the LST:
(i) the Euler genus of the surface, (ii) the number of apex
vertices, (iii) the number of vortices (called breadth in the
case of Σ-decomposition), and (iv) the depth of the vortices.
All known proofs of the LST are very complex, so aiming for
tight bounds for these parameters may seem to be a hopeless
endeavour. Yet, surprisingly, the nature of the proof makes it

possible to attain a tight bound for some of these parameters
(though not for mesh(t, r)).
Already the original proof by Robertson and Seymour, gives
an optimal bound for (i). More precisely, we know that the
excluded minor H does not embed in the surface Σ returned by
the LST. This is optimal in the sense that for every surface Σ
in which H does not embed, there exist H-minor-free graphs
with meshes for which the LST requires either the surface Σ
or a more complex one (obtained by adding handles and/or
crosscaps to Σ). Furthermore, the surface-wall constructed by
the proof ensures that for any graph H ′ embeddable in Σ, if
the parameter k is sufficiently large, then H ′ is a minor of G.
As for the apex vertices (ii), the situation is more complicated. The Flat Wall Theorem is known to hold with less than
t − 4 apex vertices [20], [30], [31], which is an optimal bound
(a grid with t − 5 apex vertices adjacent to each other and to
the vertices of the grid contains no Kt -minor). In general, the
currently known techniques give no hope for getting a bound
on the number of apex vertices which is anywhere close to
optimal, but we can bound the number of “bad” apex vertices.
Let us call an apex vertex major if it is adjacent to a vertex
which does not belong to any vortex. Dvořák and Thomas [80]
showed that if the forbidden minor H becomes planar after
deleting a vertices, then the LST is satisfied with less than a
major apex vertices (if H = Kt , then a = t − 4). This variant
has some interesting applications, including the recent proof of
the Clustered Hadwiger Conjecture [81]. Wood [82] asked if
the LST holds with polynomial bounds and less than a major
apex vertices. A positive answer to this question would imply
that Kt -minor-free graphs are (t − 1)-colourable with clusters
of size polynomial in t. We suspect that our proof can be
modified so that it has the property desired by Wood, although
in such case the breadth of the Σ-decomposition would slightly
increase.
Conjecture 6.6: There exists a version of the LST with
polynomial bounds and a number of major apices smaller than
the least integer a such that H becomes planar after deleting
a apex vertices.
Regarding (iii), the proof by Kawarabayashi et al. [18] gives
a good explicit 2t2 bound on the number of vortices. In this
paper, we get a slightly better bound of 21 (t − 3)(t − 4) by
showing that Kt is a minor of a graph which can be drawn
in the plane with 21 (t − 3)(t − 4) pairs of edges crossing. Our
proof suggests that the optimal bound is the minimum crossing
number of a graph containing H as a minor. Here, the crossing
number cr(H) of a graph H is the lowest number of edge
crossings in a drawing of H on the plane. Let cr′ (H) denote
the lowest value of cr(H ′ ) where H ′ ranges over all graphs
containing H as a minor. Note that in general cr′ (H) can be
much smaller than cr(H). For example, cr(Kt ) = Ω(t4 ) [83],
whereas cr′ (Kt ) ≤ 12 (t − 3)(t − 4), as we have shown. We
conjecture the following.
Conjecture 6.7: There exists a version of the LST with
polynomial bounds where the breadth of ρ is smaller than
cr′ (H).

Finally, the depth of the vortices. Thilikos and Wiederrecht [45] showed that the only obstruction to a vortex-free
Σ-decomposition with bounded parameters is the presence of
a “shallow vortex-grid” as a minor. There are several ways
in which we can construct obstructions to a Σ-decomposition
of small depth (see Figure 14), and it is not clear whether
there exists a nice construction of graphs characterizing graphs
admitting a Σ-decomposition of depth, say, at most 3.
Our proof yields vortices of depth depending on the parameter k. Before we ask about a tight bound on the depth, we
should ask if the depth can be bounded in terms of t alone.
We believe that this is possible.
Conjecture 6.9: The LST can be proven with polynomial
bounds and with depth of the Σ-decomposition bounded in
terms of t alone.
While we can bound the parameters of a Σ-decomposition
separately, in an optimal Σ-decomposition they probably never
need to reach the upper bounds simultaneously. We would
like to conclude the paper with a somewhat provocative
conjecture, which generalises all of the conjectures above. It
provides more fine-grained bounds on the parameters of the
Σ-decomposition returned by the LST, with bounds depending
on possible near embeddings of the forbidden minor H.
Conjecture 6.10: The LST can be proven with polynomial
bounds so that when we apply it to (H, G, M ) and it returns
(Σ, A, M ′ , ρ), then there does not exist an (a, b, w)-near
embedding of H in Σ such that a is at most the number of
major apex vertices in A, b is at most the breadth of ρ, and
w ∈ o(d) where d is the depth of ρ.
